## Solution

We find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$f(f(x+1)+y-1)=f(x)+y \quad \text{for all } x,y\in\mathbb{R}. \tag{$\star$}$$

**Step 1: Surjectivity.** Fix any $x\in\mathbb{R}$. As $y$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}$, the right-hand side $f(x)+y$ ranges over all of $\mathbb{R}$. Since the left-hand side is a value of $f$, $f$ is surjective.

**Step 2: A key identity.** In $(\star)$, set $y = z - f(x+1)+1$, where $z$ is an arbitrary real number. Then the argument of $f$ on the left becomes $f(x+1)+(z-f(x+1)+1)-1 = z$, giving
$$f(z) = f(x) + z - f(x+1) + 1 \quad \text{for all } x,z\in\mathbb{R}. \tag{1}$$

**Step 3: $f$ is affine.** Rearranging (1):
$$f(z) - z = f(x) - f(x+1) + 1 \quad \text{for all } x,z\in\mathbb{R}.$$
The left side depends only on $z$ and the right side depends only on $x$, so both sides equal a common constant $c$. Hence
$$f(z) = z + c \quad \text{for all } z\in\mathbb{R},$$
and also $f(x)-f(x+1)+1 = c$ for all $x$. Substituting $f(x)=x+c$:
$$(x+c)-(x+1+c)+1 = 0 = c.$$
Thus $c = 0$.

**Step 4: Verification.** With $f(x)=x$:
$$f(f(x+1)+y-1) = f(x+1+y-1) = x+y = f(x)+y. \quad\checkmark$$

**Conclusion.** The unique solution is $\boxed{f(x)=x}$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
